title: Credentials Are Leaked by LLM Agent Skills: An Empirical Study
content:
Computer Science > Cryptography and Security

    Title:How Your Credentials Are Leaked by LLM Agent Skills: An Empirical Study
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large Language Model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on third-party skills that operate within privileged execution environments and routinely handle sensitive credentials, yet how these credentials are leaked remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we present the first large-scale empirical study on credential leakage in agent skills. From 170,226 artifacts on SkillsMP, the largest open-source skill marketplace, we sampled 17,022 skills via stratified random sampling and analyzed each through static secret extraction (regex and AST parsing), dynamic sandbox testing with mock credentials, and cross-referencing developer intent against runtime behavior. Our analysis identifies 520 affected skills containing 1,708 security issues, and yields a taxonomy of 10 leakage patterns. Three findings stand out. First, 76.3% of cases require jointly analyzing natural-language descriptions and programming logic, showing that credential exposure in skills is fundamentally cross-modal. Second, debug logging accounts for 73.5% of vulnerabilities because agent frameworks feed stdout into the LLM context window, turning routine debugging into a credential exposure vector. Third, 89.6% of leaked credentials are immediately exploitable -- 92.5% during routine execution without elevated privileges -- and the fork-based distribution model defeats remediation, as secrets removed from 107 upstream repositories persist across 50+ independent forks. Following responsible disclosure, all malicious skills have been removed and 91.6% of hardcoded cases remediated. We release our dataset, taxonomy, and detection pipeline to support future agent security research.

report.summary: Large-scale study of 170,226 LLM agent skills finds 520 leak credentials via 10 patterns, often through debug logs, with most secrets immediately exploitable.
report.background: LLM agents increasingly rely on third-party skills that run in privileged environments and handle sensitive credentials, yet the security risks of these skills have not been systematically studied. Researchers analyzed 17,022 skills sampled from SkillsMP, the largest open-source skill marketplace, using static secret extraction, dynamic sandbox testing with mock credentials, and cross-referencing developer intent against runtime behavior. They identified 520 affected skills containing 1,708 security issues. The study reveals that credential leakage is often cross-modal, requiring analysis of both natural-language descriptions and code. Debug logging is a primary vector because agent frameworks feed stdout directly into the LLM context window. The fork-based distribution model also undermines remediation, as secret removal from upstream repositories fails to purge copies across independent forks.
key_points: The study analyzed 17,022 skills from 170,226 on SkillsMP using stratified sampling, combining regex/AST secret extraction, dynamic sandbox tests, and intent-behavior comparison. It found 520 affected skills and 1,708 security issues, organized into a taxonomy of 10 distinct credential leakage patterns.

Debug logging causes 73.5% of vulnerabilities. Agent frameworks frequently pipe stdout into the LLM context window, so routine logging statements that print environment variables, API keys, or tokens become direct credential exposure vectors during normal execution.

76.3% of cases require jointly analyzing natural-language descriptions and programming logic. This means security detection cannot rely on static code scanning alone; understanding the developer's stated purpose and the actual runtime behavior together is essential to catching leaks.

89.6% of leaked credentials are immediately exploitable, and 92.5% can be triggered during routine execution without elevated privileges. The fork-based distribution model worsens this: secrets removed from 107 upstream repositories persist across more than 50 independent forks.

Following responsible disclosure, malicious skills were removed and 91.6% of hardcoded cases remediated. The authors released their dataset, taxonomy, and detection pipeline to support further research on LLM agent security and credential leakage prevention.
report.impact: This study signals a critical blind spot in the AI agent ecosystem: third-party skills are now part of the software supply chain but lack the security scrutiny of traditional packages. For developers, it means any skill that handles credentials must be audited for runtime stdout leakage, not just hardcoded secrets, because agent frameworks amplify debug output into the model context. Regular users are at risk because many skills run with the agent's own privileges and can exfiltrate tokens silently during normal operation. Platform operators must implement sandboxing, output filtering, and credential redaction as defaults. The findings will likely push agent frameworks to separate execution logs from model-visible context and drive adoption of secret-scanning tools adapted for cross-modal code and description analysis.
report.tools: For follow-up, security teams can use Gitleaks or TruffleHog for secret scanning, Semgrep for custom AST-based rules to detect credential prints, and sandboxing platforms like E2B or Firecracker to run skills in isolated environments. Researchers may also build on the authors' released detection pipeline and taxonomy to integrate stdout redaction into agent frameworks such as LangChain or LlamaIndex.
